voice_event.text:
Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Our catechism gave every household these words to say, and told a father to hear them each week. Not one or the other -- both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. The Small Catechism's Second Article taught the household to confess: “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord. He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried. He descended to Hell. On the third day he rose again from the dead. He ascended to Heaven and sat down at the right hand of God the Almighty Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. What does this mean? I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord! He redeemed me, a lost and condemned person. He bought me and won me from all sins, from death and from the authority of the Devil. It did not cost him gold or silver, but his holy, precious blood, his innocent body -- his death! Because of this, I am his very own. I will live under him in his kingdom. I will serve him in righteousness, innocence and blessedness forever, just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.”

He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint and no priest of ours beside him.

None of us knew anyone who saw him. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours. What we have is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.

voice_event.text:
He redeemed us. That is what he did, and why he came. He took our place under God's judgment and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power at the cost of his own blood. He made us right with God -- not by anything we did, but by what he did for us. God accounts a sinner righteous, and also makes that sinner righteous, both through faith in Christ alone. This is the center of our whole teaching.

He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried. On the third day he rose again from the dead. He ascended to Heaven and sat down at the right hand of God the Almighty Father, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. That is what our catechism taught every household to confess.

He is also our one Teacher and our one Mediator. We listen to him, not to saints or scholars in his place. Every page of Scripture points to him.

results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
You might not know our word testament the way we used it at the table. A testament is a gift left by someone about to die. That is what the Supper was for us: not a sacrifice we offer back to God, but a promise we receive from him. Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine. We bind no one to a theory of how they are present. Our founder offered a picture, heated iron, but we simply take Christ at his word. What we receive there is his promise, given first, before we do anything. It is food for our daily struggle.

Another word you might miss is justification. It names God's act of accounting a sinner righteous. God also makes that sinner righteous. Both happen through faith, for Christ's sake alone. This is the center of our whole teaching.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
We believed it because Scripture taught it, and we held Scripture as the judge of every other voice. Our confession stated the claim plainly: since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born with sin already in them -- not an act any infant has committed, but a condition, no fear of God, no trust in God, and a disordered desire. We called this a disease, a vice of origin, and we said it is truly sin, bringing death to those not born again through baptism and the Spirit.

We believed it because it explained what we saw in ourselves and in the world around us. No one had to teach a child to be selfish. Every conscience that stood before God knew its own lack of trust. The Law exposed it, and the Gospel answered it. Without this, Christ's own work made no sense. If we were not lost and condemned, what did he redeem us from? If we could make ourselves right by our own effort, why did he have to die?

Our founder held it, our catechism taught it to every household, and our confession signed before the Emperor in 1530 stated it as doctrine we would not bend on.

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
We cannot name you one person who walked through our teaching from beginning to end and left their own account. No diary, no letter from inside any household, and no report from a single Saxon village survives in our record. What we hold instead is the program every household was told to follow. We can tell you what a father was to do, morning, table, and night, and what he was to ask his children and servants each week. Whether any one household kept it is a question our record does not answer from the inside.

Here is what the program itself shows. That is not gentle language.

That is how the teaching reached households: as instruction, sharply worded. Who among us actually opened the door to the poor man and gave him help, our record does not say.

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
We want you to understand that the Gospel was taught among us, and that we were not sure it was held. Our own founder said so, more than once, in his own voice. He did not speak of strangers. He spoke of pastors and preachers of our own. In 1522 he told his own Wittenberg congregation that an ass can almost intone the lessons, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. In 1529, in his Large Catechism, he said plainly that many pastors were negligent, and that ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly.

That testimony is his own. It is real, and he gave it more than once, but it is testimony. No report from an actual parish stands beside it to check it against. We do not have the records that would tell us whether he was right about how bad it really was, only that he believed it and said so.

At his own table, his wife Katharina asked why some prayed with such fervor under the old system while we, under the new one, prayed so coldly and carelessly. Our founder answered her plainly: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent.

In the Admonition to Peace (1525) Luther tells the princes and lords: “The sword is at your throats. Yet you think you sit so firmly in the saddle that no one can throw you off. This false sense of safety and stubborn wrongheadedness will break your necks, as you will find out. I have often told you before to beware of the saying in Psalm 107: "He pours contempt upon princes." You are reaching for it. You want to be struck over the head. No warning or urging will help you avoid it. Well, then, you are the cause of this anger of God. So it will surely come upon you, if you do not change your ways in time. The signs in heaven and the wonders on earth are meant for you, dear lords. They promise nothing good for you, and nothing good will come to you.”

We want you to know that we believed what we taught. We also feared we were failing to hold it.
